note: Argues against the efficiency only narrative and for human complementary deployment, a useful counterweight in strategy work.
title: Human-AI agency in the age of generative AI
explain_beginner: Much of the public conversation about generative AI, tools like chatbots that write text or code, focuses on efficiency, meaning how much time or cost a company can save by letting AI do work a person used to do. This paper pushes back on that narrow framing. It argues that the more important story is what happens when people and AI work together, with humans still actively steering, questioning, and combining ideas rather than simply handing tasks over. The author looks at generative AI through several lenses at once, as a tool useful for almost any kind of work, as a spark for trying new and unusual ideas rather than just doing familiar tasks faster, as a way to bring more varied perspectives into a team's thinking, and as something that is becoming easier for more people to use regardless of technical skill. The central claim is that how much value organizations and society get from generative AI, and how fairly those gains get shared, depends heavily on the choices leaders and policymakers make, not on the technology by itself.
explain_business: For a business leader evaluating generative AI, this paper's message cuts against the common pitch of pure cost or headcount savings. The author argues that generative AI's real upside for a company comes less from replacing tasks and more from what it enables when paired with active human involvement, including exploring unfamiliar ideas rather than only optimizing familiar ones, drawing in more varied perspectives across a team, and lowering the skill barrier so more employees, not just specialists, can use advanced AI capability. The practical implication is that organizations designing generative AI rollouts purely around efficiency metrics and job cuts may miss the technology's larger value, and that how gains are distributed across a workforce depends on deliberate managerial and policy choices rather than happening automatically. This is a conceptual argument, not a set of measured outcomes or a return on investment case study, so it works best as a framing tool for leadership discussions about strategy and workforce design, rather than as a source of hard numbers to justify a specific deployment decision.
explain_practitioner: This is a conceptual paper rather than an empirical study, developing an argument about human-AI agency using generative AI and management scholarship rather than new data collection. The author frames generative AI along four dimensions: a general-purpose technology applicable across domains, a catalyst for exploratory innovation rather than only efficiency gains, a mechanism for expanding cognitive diversity within organizations, and a technology with democratizing potential for who can use advanced AI capability. The core theoretical move is treating generative AI as meaningfully different from earlier predictive or optimization focused AI, arguing it requires renewed attention to human agency, meaning active human judgment and steering, rather than the passive efficiency-only framing common in prior AI discourse. The result that matters is the claim that human agency determines whether generative AI's gains in creativity, innovation, and growth are captured broadly or narrowly, making managerial and policy choices, not the technology itself, the deciding factor. Because the paper is conceptual, its main limitation is that claims about creativity, diversity, and democratization gains are argued theoretically rather than tested against organizational data.
